stories.title: China evacuates tens of thousands as rain from Typhoon Narra lashes southwest
stories.summary: Torrential rain triggered by Typhoon Narra caused widespread flooding across China's southwestern Guangxi region over the weekend, forcing tens of thousands of people to relocate as forecasters warned of more downpours in the days ahead. Some 54,000 people have been relocated because of the flooding, including 8,087 moved to emergency shelters, state broadcaster CCTV said. Water levels at 20 monitoring stations on 15 rivers exceeded warning thresholds. Aerial footage from CCTV showed brown floodwaters engulfing parts of Chongzuo city, with roads and clusters of low-rise buildings submerged. Rescuers could be seen wading through knee-deep floodwaters while using rubber boats to evacuate stranded residents from inundated neighbourhoods. Typhoon Narra has lingered over the Beibu Gulf, also known as the Gulf of Tonkin, in the northwestern part of the South China Sea for several days, bringing heavy rain to Guangxi and the nearby provinces of Hainan and Guangdong. Heavy rain is expected to persist across parts of southern China through Wednesday, with areas of Guangxi, Guangdong, Hainan and Fujian forecast to receive torrential rain, CCTV said. China postponed the launch of its uncrewed Chang'e-7 lunar mission, which had been expected as early as Monday from Hainan's Wenchang Space Launch Site, saying the spacecraft did not "meet launch conditions." The National Astronomical Research Institute of Thailand, which has a scientific payload aboard the mission, said the delay was caused by the typhoon.

stories.title: New coalition of states could form around Trans-Arctic Corridor — expert
stories.summary: Irina Strelnikova, director of the Center for Interdisciplinary Arctic Studies at the Higher School of Economics, said that China, India, and the United Arab Emirates could become potential participants in this alliance
article_sentences: MOSCOW, August 24.

A new coalition of states could form around the development of the Trans-Arctic transport corridor, which is already turning into not only an economic but also a geopolitical project, Irina Strelnikova, director of the Center for Interdisciplinary Arctic Studies at the Higher School of Economics, told TASS.
"The scenario is entirely realistic.

There are certain caveats to consider, but I would say that it is already taking shape as a geopolitical project, and the economic component, indeed, is gaining momentum alongside the geopolitical one," she said when asked about the potential formation of a new coalition of states centered on the Trans-Arctic transport corridor.

China, India, and the United Arab Emirates could become potential participants in this alliance, Strelnikova said, adding that Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan are also showing interest in expanding transport chains and accessing new markets.
Forming a stable coalition requires an alignment of the states’ economic interests, the expert noted.
The project must offer tangible benefits to participants, including access to resources, new markets, and the development of logistics capabilities.
Strelnikova cited political will and the readiness of states to reach agreements on contentious issues as another condition.
In particular, she believes potential coalition members need to set aside their differences regarding the legal status of the Northern Sea Route.

The expert also mentioned geopolitical competition, US sanctions pressure, and the risk of fragmented cooperation, whereby instead of a unified coalition, separate partnerships between Russia and China, India, and the UAE would develop, as potential obstacles.

stories.title: New Zealand to introduce bill banning social media for children under 16
stories.summary: SYDNEY, Aug 24 - New Zealand's conservative coalition government will introduce a bill in Parliament on Monday that seeks to ban children under 16 from using social media, and proposes fines of up to 10% of a platform's global revenue for non-compliance.
article_sentences: New Zealand's conservative coalition government will introduce a bill in Parliament on Monday that seeks to ban children under 16 from using social media, and proposes fines of up to 10% of a platform's global revenue for non-compliance.
The bill would require social media platforms to take reasonable steps to verify users' ages, including by using existing account information, facial technology and digital identity documents.
"We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said in a statement.
